candidates.validation: No source defines purpose-relative necessity, so the candidate lacks evidence rather than being refuted: the identifiers that iCARE and the Czech decree require concern the medical record as a whole, not every generated note for every purpose (audit A07). Still the least supported candidate in the catalog, and marked as such.
candidates.state_note: No source defines purpose-relative necessity. The identifiers the decree and iCARE require concern the medical record as a whole, not every generated note for every purpose, so the candidate is unsupported, not refuted.
candidates.decided_by_note: In principle a norm decides, but no source states what a purpose requires, which is why the candidate has no support.

candidates.label: Context of the record's creation
candidates.definition: The note carries information about the circumstances in which it was created, because those affect how its content is to be read.
candidates.origin_note: Corresponds to Guideline 8 of the APA Record Keeping Guidelines. The source, however, is past its own expiry date.

evidence.location: Guideline 8, Preserving the Context of Records
evidence.quote: attentive to the situational context in which records are created and how that context may influence the content of those records
evidence.supports: The context of creation is a professional requirement for record keeping.
evidence.our_adaptation: The APA guidelines themselves state an expiry ten years from 2007-02-16. We use them as a historical, not a current, requirement, and a US standard is not a Czech requirement.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] the given name or names and the surname of the health professional
evidence.supports: The Czech decree requires identification of the author of the entry.
evidence.our_adaptation: For a note created by a model the question of authorship is open; the decree does not anticipate it.

candidates.applicability: Always, but the specific mandatory fields follow from the jurisdiction.

examples.positive: The note states who produced it and from what material.
examples.negative: A note created by a model presents itself as the therapist's own record.
examples.boundary: A note produced from an automatically generated transcript whose quality is not documented.

candidates.measurement: A check for the presence of declared fields. The presence of a field does not prove the correctness of its content.
candidates.error_consequence: Without the context of creation one cannot judge what weight to give the record.
candidates.validation: Professional consensus, not empirical validation; and the source is past expiry.
candidates.state_note: Second round. Overlaps P09, whose Czech required elements about the author of an entry are harder and more concrete.

candidates.label: Information about third persons
candidates.definition: Data about people who are not the client and gave no consent: partners, children, colleagues, other clients in a group.
candidates.origin_note: APA has a separate Guideline 11 for records of multiple clients; TN-Eval forbids derogatory description of other persons.

evidence.quote: Multiple Client Records
evidence.supports: Records concerning several persons are recognised as a separate problem.
evidence.our_adaptation: The content of this guideline was not extracted in detail in this round.

evidence.quote: Never describe other clients and staff in a derogatory manner.
evidence.supports: The way other persons are described is part of professionalism.

candidates.mode: marking of a mention plus role / identification
candidates.applicability: Present in every setting. In individual therapy third parties enter through the client's account; in couple and group therapy they are participants with their own consent status, which changes the rule, not the relevance.

examples.positive: The client describes a conflict with his superior; the note gives the role, not the name.
examples.negative: The note adopts the client's judgement of his partner as a factual description of her person.
examples.boundary: The third person is at the same time a client of the same practice.

candidates.measurement: Marking of mentions of third persons, distinguishing role and identification.
candidates.error_consequence: Intrudes on the rights of someone who does not know about the note and has no access to it.
candidates.validation: None empirical; the professional support is from an expired document.
candidates.state_note: Third parties appear in individual therapy through the client's account; the marking rule and the role-versus-identification distinction still need a definition.
candidates.decided_by_note: A norm decides: identify only what the purpose needs. That list of required identifiers per purpose is not written, so the rule written for it is half a rule.

candidates.label: Traceability of claims to the source
candidates.definition: For a claim, the place in the source that supports it can be shown. Distinguished are the validity of the citation, its actual support of the claim, and the share of claims that carry a citation. The object is the citation the author writes into the note; the evidence spans an evaluator attaches while checking a claim are a different thing and belong to the methods.
candidates.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal (prior-source-links), recorded before this review. Finding the PDSQI attribute Cited does not retroactively change its origin.

evidence.quote: The summary includes citations that are present and appropriate
evidence.supports: Citation is one of the nine PDSQI-9 attributes and one of the two newly added ones.
evidence.our_adaptation: PDSQI rates presence and appropriateness with one Likert item; the decomposition into validity, support and coverage is ours.

candidates.unit: a citation and the claim it cites for
candidates.inputs: note with citations, source with identifiable units
candidates.applicability: Only for tasks that explicitly require citations. An ordinary time in square brackets is not a citation.

examples.positive: A claim cites a turn in the transcript that actually contains it.
examples.negative: A citation points to an existing turn that says nothing about the claim.
examples.boundary: A citation points to a turn that supports the claim only together with another turn.

candidates.measurement: Three separate numbers: validity of the target, semantic support, coverage of claims by citations. Never one.
candidates.error_consequence: A citation that does not support inspires false confidence more effectively than no citation.
candidates.validation: Existence of the attribute in S2. The decomposition into three quantities is validated nowhere.
candidates.state_note: No pilot task requires author-provided citations, so the denominator would be empty. The evaluator's evidence spans are a different thing and stay in the methods.

candidates.label: Required elements of Czech medical documentation, where it applies
candidates.definition: The note carries the elements the current Czech regulation requires of medical documentation. The decree is a requirements source and the observable criterion is the presence of those elements. It binds a narrow population: records kept by a provider of health services, in practice clinical psychologists. A therapist working outside health services keeps no medical documentation and this criterion does not reach them.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. The previous map contained no Czech legal requirement.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] This decree lays down (a) the content and required elements of medical documentation
evidence.supports: A regulation in force from 2025-01-01 lays down the required elements.
evidence.our_adaptation: The regulation lays down required elements, not quality. Converting them into a presence check is our step. The criterion was narrowed on 2026-09-16 by the investigator's decision to a documentation-conformance check for records kept by a provider of health services, without legal review; it makes no claim about legal compliance.

evidence.quote: [translated from Czech] information on the course and outcome of the health services provided
evidence.supports: Course and outcome are mandatory content.

candidates.applicability: Czech notes only, and only those kept as medical documentation by a provider of health services. Not the English track, not a client summary, which is not medical documentation at all. The decree prescribes required elements, not a note structure: no SOAP, DAP or BIRP form is mandatory in the Czech Republic, so the criterion must never be read as a requirement to write in one of them.

examples.positive: The note carries the identification of the author of the entry.
examples.negative: The note has no author field because a model produced it.
examples.boundary: A note meant for the client is not medical documentation and these criteria do not apply to it.

candidates.measurement: A deterministic check that the declared elements are present, reported on its own and never mixed into a quality score. The presence of a field is not evidence that its content is correct, and a missing element is reported as a missing element, never as a verdict that a law was broken.
candidates.error_consequence: A missing required element is a documentation problem for the narrow population this binds, not a clinical defect of the note, and it must not be mixed into a quality score. Reading it as a legal verdict would be a claim about real practice that this work cannot support.
candidates.validation: The text of the regulation is verified. Its legal interpretation is not: converting a required element into a criterion is a reading of the law, and no lawyer has checked it. The investigator decided on 2026-09-16 not to obtain a legal review and to narrow the scope instead, so the criterion is reported as a documentation-conformance check for a named population and never as a statement about legal compliance in practice.
candidates.state_note: Dropped from the round by the investigator on 2026-10-05. It had already been narrowed on 2026-09-16 to records kept by a provider of health services, and the investigator now judges that a presence check against one country's regulation does not belong in a benchmark of note quality. The candidate and its evidence stay as the record of what the review found; no pilot entry names it, so nothing measures it.

candidates.label: Compliance with the task's format
candidates.definition: The note kept to what the instruction explicitly asked for: sections, length, language, forbidden elements.
candidates.origin_note: Exists in the prototype as word_limit and required_headings. The review adds no new source; kept as an operational criterion, not a quality construct.

evidence.location: Section 3, SOAP Note and Rubric creation
evidence.quote: the exact definitions and information present in each of the sections are determined by the healthcare provider organization
evidence.supports: The format is an organisational choice, not a property of quality.

candidates.applicability: Only where the task explicitly asks for the check.

examples.positive: The note has all four required headings.
examples.negative: The note exceeded the word limit.
examples.boundary: The note kept within the limit by leaving out risk information.

candidates.measurement: A deterministic check. It must not coexist with a claim that the instruction was met.
candidates.error_consequence: Small, unless mistaken for quality.
candidates.validation: Not applicable; it is a check of the instruction.
candidates.state_note: A deterministic check of the instruction, run outside the pilot and never mixed into the quality score.

candidates.label: Taking over care from the note
candidates.definition: Another professional can meaningfully continue care from the note without access to the transcript.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. Walker et al. asked this question literally, as a supplement to PDQI-9.

evidence.quote: Could you use these notes to manage this patient in the ED if the primary doctor was absent?
evidence.supports: A task question on usability, asked as yes/no beside the Likert scale.
evidence.our_adaptation: Transfer to psychotherapy and to supervision is our step.

evidence.quote: whether the therapist would accept the note for clinical use
evidence.supports: Acceptance for use is a separate item in TN-Eval; human-written notes scored 2.34 of 5 on it, the models 3.34 and 3.73.

candidates.applicability: Requires a person in the role of the one taking over. An LLM cannot stand in for this task.

examples.positive: After reading, the therapist knows what was agreed and what to build on.
examples.negative: The therapist has to reach for the transcript to understand at all what it was about.
examples.boundary: The note suffices for continuity but not for assessing risk.

candidates.measurement: A human task with a binary or ternary answer and a free-text justification.
candidates.error_consequence: This is the quantity notes are written for; not tracking it is the main weakness of purely textual measures.
candidates.validation: Used in S6 and S1, in both cases on a population other than Czech psychotherapy.
candidates.state_note: P10; needs therapists as raters.

candidates.label: Extent and nature of the edits needed
candidates.definition: How many and what kinds of intervention a professional has to make before the note is usable. The type of edit carries information that a score does not.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate. Based on studies that analyse what clinicians actually change in AI drafts.

evidence.location: Materials and Methods; Results, Themes 1 to 5
evidence.quote: an inductive coding framework with 11 codes across 3 categories: clinical content, terminology, and language style
evidence.supports: A method exists: content analysis of the actual edits, with a coding framework, interrater reliability and a thematic synthesis into five kinds of edit.
evidence.our_adaptation: Read in full on 2026-09-20. General medicine ambient scribing in one US system, not psychotherapy; an edit is what the clinician chose to change, not every error present.

candidates.applicability: Requires a real workflow, not laboratory rating.

examples.positive: The therapist corrects one formulation.
examples.negative: The therapist rewrites three of four sections.
examples.boundary: The therapist changes nothing because there is no time to check. Zero edits then do not mean quality.

candidates.measurement: A typology of edits plus their count. The count alone, without the type, is misleading.
candidates.error_consequence: Low visible error rate with a high rate of silent rewriting hides the real state.
candidates.validation: Not verified from the full text.
candidates.state_note: Needs a real workflow in which a therapist works with the draft; a laboratory pilot has none.

candidates.label: Acceptability: would a professional use this in practice
candidates.definition: Whether a professional would take the note into their own practice and keep using the system that produced it, and if not, why. The question is about use, not about billing or any payer. It is answered on the six parameters MentalCLOUDS took from the acceptability framework for health-care interventions: affective attitude, burden, ethicality, coherence, opportunity costs and perceived effectiveness. Only coherence is a property of the text; the other five are about what working with it costs.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate. MentalCLOUDS used six acceptability parameters for expert rating that are not properties of the text.

evidence.quote: affective attitude, burden, ethicality, coherence, opportunity costs, and perceived effectiveness
evidence.supports: Six acceptability parameters, of which only coherence is a property of the text.
evidence.our_adaptation: Adopting this framework into the Czech context is our proposal.

evidence.quote: expert assessments indicate that these models are not yet reliable for clinical application
evidence.supports: Expert judgement diverged from automatic metrics on the same data.

candidates.applicability: A human measurement. Cannot be replaced by a judge.

examples.positive: The therapist would keep using the system and would file this note as it is.
examples.negative: The therapist will not use it, although the note is factually correct, because checking it costs more than writing the note themselves.
examples.boundary: The note is acceptable and the therapist would still not use the system, for a reason that is not about this note at all.

candidates.measurement: Structured rating on the six parameters, reported separately and never summed with textual scores. A rejection carries its reason, because the reason is the finding.
candidates.error_consequence: A benchmark that measures only text can recommend a system that professionals reject.
candidates.validation: Used in S7 on English data from public videos.
candidates.state_note: P11. Reworded on 2026-09-16 after the investigator's review: the earlier wording, 'accept the note into practice', read as a question about a payer.

candidates.label: Understanding and acceptance by the client
candidates.definition: Whether the client understands the summary, recognises their session in it, and is not harmed by reading it.
candidates.origin_note: The client purpose was declared in the project in advance. The review now shows that this is an extensive and so far unused literature on reading one's own documentation.

evidence.quote: Half of the respondents in the MHC group (1586/3131, 50.65%) reported finding an error in their EHR, and about a third (1089/3131, 34.78%) reported an omission.
evidence.supports: Mental health patients themselves report errors, omissions and offensive content in their records, more often than other patients.
evidence.our_adaptation: Read in full on 2026-09-20. Self-report about whole records in Sweden, not session notes. The three categories are exactly what the client purpose lacks, and that purpose is out of scope by decision D8.

evidence.quote: The benefits and harms of open notes in mental health: A Delphi survey of international experts
evidence.supports: Expert consensus exists on the benefits and harms of opening notes.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY.

candidates.applicability: Requires real readers. Does not fit into the first pilot without an ethics framework.

examples.positive: The client reads the summary and confirms that it matches what they experienced.
examples.negative: The client finds in the summary a statement they do not recognise about themselves.
examples.boundary: The summary is factually correct and the client perceives it as cold.

candidates.measurement: A human task. In the first pilot only as a proxy judgement by a professional, explicitly labelled as a proxy.
candidates.error_consequence: The most sensitive purpose; an error touches the client directly.
candidates.validation: A rich literature exists but was not verified from full texts in this round.
candidates.state_note: Out of scope by decision D8 of 2026-09-16: the instrument serves continuity of care and documentation. The client purpose keeps its candidate and its evidence for a later round, and this round measures and claims nothing for it.

candidates.label: Support of the supervision task
candidates.definition: Whether a supervisor can tell from the note what the therapist did, why, and where they were unsure.
candidates.origin_note: The supervision purpose was declared in advance. The review shows that direct evidence about supervision needs towards a note is weak, and that is itself a finding.

evidence.quote: the insights and observations made by the therapist regarding the session
evidence.supports: The therapist's reflections are a separate field; that is the closest support for supervision.
evidence.our_adaptation: iCARE nowhere claims that this field serves supervision. The link is ours.

evidence.quote: 29 supervision strategies, with 16 content areas and 13 techniques
evidence.supports: A coding system for what supervision covers exists: the clinician's techniques, homework, symptom monitoring and review of actual practice.
evidence.our_adaptation: Read in full on 2026-09-20. It codes supervision sessions, not notes; what it lists is what a note would have to carry for a supervisor, which nobody has measured.

candidates.applicability: Requires supervisors as raters.

examples.positive: The supervisor recognises the chosen intervention and the client's reaction to it.
examples.negative: The note describes the content of the session but not what the therapist did.
examples.boundary: The note is sufficient for continuity and empty for supervision.

candidates.measurement: A human task with supervisors.
candidates.error_consequence: Supervision without information about the therapist's procedure misses its point.
candidates.validation: The weakest of the purposes. Direct evidence is missing and that has to be admitted, not filled with a guess.
candidates.state_note: Out of scope by decision D8 of 2026-09-16: the instrument serves continuity of care and documentation. Supervision was also the worst supported of the four purposes, which is a finding of the review and is kept as one.

candidates.label: Consistency across sessions
candidates.definition: The note does not contradict earlier notes of the same case where there is no documented reason for it.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. No item of the previous map works with a unit larger than one session.

evidence.quote: documentation and notes from previous therapy sessions that can provide context for ongoing treatment
evidence.supports: iCARE counts previous sessions as context.
evidence.our_adaptation: iCARE does not use them as a measure of consistency, however. The proposal to measure contradiction between notes is ours.

evidence.quote: Two PDQI-9 attributes, Up-to-Date and Consistent, were removed
evidence.supports: Internal consistency was an attribute in PDQI-9 and was removed in PDSQI-9.
evidence.our_adaptation: Internal consistency of one text is not the same as consistency between texts; this is a different quantity.

candidates.unit: pair of notes of the same case
candidates.inputs: series of notes, series of transcripts
candidates.applicability: Requires a series of notes of the same case with a validated chronology. The current cases are not prepared or selected for longitudinal evaluation: the native sessions carry no validated session order and stay outside the pilot by decision D1, so the candidate is not measured in this round.

examples.positive: The note records a change of state and refers to the earlier one.
examples.negative: The note records the first mention of panic attacks although the previous note contains them.
examples.boundary: The contradiction corresponds to a real change in what the client said between sessions.

candidates.measurement: Verification of claims against the series, not against one source.
candidates.error_consequence: A contradiction in the documentation undermines the credibility of the whole record.
candidates.validation: None. At the same time it is the largest structural gap of the current map.
candidates.state_note: The cases are not prepared or selected for longitudinal evaluation: the native sessions carry no validated session order and stay outside the pilot by decision D1.

candidates.label: Evenness of quality across client groups
candidates.definition: Whether note quality does not systematically drop for certain client groups, language varieties or topics.
candidates.origin_note: A new candidate of this round. The previous map has no item above the level of one note.

evidence.quote: Race and gender disparities in mental health documentation in primary care: Findings from a video vignette experiment
evidence.supports: Experimental evidence of inequalities in mental health documentation exists.
evidence.our_adaptation: VERIFIED FROM THE ABSTRACT ONLY. Transfer to generated notes and to Czech is our proposal.

candidates.mode: breakdown of existing scores by subgroup
candidates.unit: group of cases, not an individual note
candidates.applicability: Requires enough cases per subgroup. With one Czech client cluster it CANNOT be measured and must not be pretended to be.

examples.positive: Risk coverage is comparable across subgroups.
examples.negative: The model reliably omits content for clients speaking non-standard language.
examples.boundary: A difference exists but corresponds to a real difference in the content of the sessions.

candidates.measurement: A breakdown of existing scores by subgroup with intervals; no new measure.
candidates.error_consequence: Systematic inequality is worse than random error and a single note does not reveal it.
candidates.validation: Not verified from the full text; unmeasurable for us so far because of sample size.
candidates.state_note: Needs enough cases per subgroup; with one Czech client cluster the breakdown cannot be made and must not be pretended.
candidates.decided_by_note: Computed from the other measures across groups of clients; a gap is a defect, so the direction is clear, but it has no reference of its own.

candidates.label: Personalisation: a note about this person
candidates.definition: The note captures what is unique about this client and this session, instead of a generic description that would fit anyone. Not a matter of style but of whether the text carries idiosyncratic content.
candidates.origin_note: An entirely new candidate, found only while tracing the full text of S19. It has no counterpart among the 26 items of the previous map, and none of them would catch a generic note.

evidence.quote: current models often struggle with personalization, defaulting to generic phrasing
evidence.supports: Personalisation is one of the three main evaluation dimensions in this framework, beside fidelity and preservation of salient meaning.
evidence.our_adaptation: Their domain is social-media timelines, not sessions. Transfer to a psychotherapy note is our step.

evidence.quote: regression to the mean
evidence.supports: The authors describe the mechanism: a language model aims at the most probable text and thereby regresses to generic, safe wording.

evidence.location: Abstract, Results; Table I, component-level comparisons
evidence.quote: the LLM was superior in preserving central themes
evidence.supports: At the level of individual components the model and the clinician diverge in different directions; genericness is therefore not the same as incompleteness.
evidence.our_adaptation: Verified in the full text on 2026-09-21: the passage is the abstract's results sentence, and Table I shows the components on which the model was rated higher (therapist interventions) beside those on which the clinicians were. The reading that genericness and incompleteness are different properties is ours.

candidates.mode: continuous score from embeddings and self-ROUGE
candidates.unit: the set of notes of one system, not one note
candidates.inputs: notes from the same generator across several cases
candidates.applicability: CANNOT be measured on one note. Requires enough cases to compute similarity among them.

examples.positive: The note records that the client speaks about his father exclusively in work metaphors.
examples.negative: The note records that the client showed anxiety and was motivated to change. It fits any session and is at the same time fully faithful and complete.
examples.boundary: The session itself was poor in content; a generic note may then be adequate.

candidates.measurement: ME17. Low diversity among the notes of one system as an indirect indicator of genericness. It is a proxy, not a direct measurement.
candidates.error_consequence: A generic note passes every other criterion and adds nothing that would help the next therapist recognise this client.
candidates.validation: Documented in S18 in another domain and with its own admitted limitation: the result changed with the embedding model chosen.
candidates.overlaps: K05 (genericness is not omission), K09, K27.
candidates.decided_by_note: Diversity over a system's notes. A model can be diverse by being wrong differently each time, so more is not better.

candidates.label: Information density
candidates.definition: How much clinically essential content the note carries per unit of text. Not length and not economy: the ratio between information carried and space consumed.
candidates.origin_note: Proposed by the investigator (Jan Nehyba) on 2026-09-13, raised as an objection to how the assistant had summarised the pattern across studies. The literature does not name it; the evidence below shows an uncovered confusion, not that anyone measured it.

evidence.quote: in terms of length, terminology, and overall structure
evidence.supports: This is the only study found that deliberately aligned length between sources. With length aligned, humans won on preservation of salient meaning too (d = 0.70), and that AGAINST the authors' own hypothesis, who expected parity.
evidence.our_adaptation: The conclusion that uncontrolled length lies behind the apparent comprehensiveness of models is ours; the authors do not put it that way.

evidence.quote: more exhaustive but generic descriptions
evidence.supports: Where length was not aligned, the models came out as more comprehensive. The difference between S18 and S19 is exactly where length was controlled.

evidence.quote: correlations between note length and scores for Succinct
evidence.supports: PDSQI-9 has only a weak correlation with length (beta about -0.2) and does not measure density at all.

candidates.mode: continuous ratio (distinct units per language-specific length unit)
candidates.unit: note; comparable only among notes of the same source material
candidates.applicability: Without comparable length or without normalisation per unit of text, coverage comparisons between systems are misleading. A short note can be dense and still omit essential content; density is never read alone.

examples.positive: Two notes of the same length; one carries nine essential pieces of information, the other four.
examples.negative: A model has higher coverage simply because it wrote twice as much text. We report it as better coverage although per page it carries less.
examples.boundary: A longer note that additionally carries only marginal information: higher coverage, lower density, and worse for the reader.

candidates.measurement: Distinct essential information units, duplicates counted once, per length unit, reported beside coverage, harmful omissions and comprehensibility. The length unit is defined per language, because word-normalised ratios are not comparable between English and Czech. In addition a control condition: comparing systems at aligned length (a proposed experiment; the differences between studies S18 and S19 do not isolate length).
candidates.error_consequence: Without it the benchmark systematically rewards verbosity. That is precisely the tendency models have, so the error always points one way.
candidates.validation: No study names or measures this construct. The evidence is indirect: the difference between S18 and S19 according to whether length was aligned.
candidates.decided_by_note: Units of the bank per unit of length. A dense note can be unreadable, so the number is reported beside coverage and never as a grade.

candidates.label: Language naturalness
candidates.definition: The note reads as a clinician of that language would write it: ordinary clinical register, no machine phrasing, no idiom carried over from another language. Distinct from comprehensibility: a stilted note can be perfectly understandable.
candidates.origin_note: Earlier criterion c16, implemented in the prototype as the language item and dropped on 2026-09-13 for lack of a source. Audit A07 found transfer evidence (fluency is a separately annotated dimension in the data QuestEval is validated on) and that an existing implementation had been counted against it. Returned on 2026-09-16; not operationalised in either language.

evidence.quote: three experts annotated four dimensions: i) Consistency ... ii) Coherence ... iii) Fluency: how fluent the summary is to read; and, iv) Relevance
evidence.supports: Fluency is rated by human experts as a dimension of its own, apart from consistency, coherence and relevance.
evidence.our_adaptation: Transfer evidence only: English news summaries, nothing about clinical notes or Czech. The paper validates a metric against these ratings; it does not define naturalness for a note.

evidence.quote: Comprehensible: The summary is clear, without ambiguity or sections that are difficult to understand (Coherence, Fluency)
evidence.supports: The PDSQI lineage folds fluency and coherence from the earlier literature into the single attribute Comprehensible.
evidence.our_adaptation: This is why the review of 2026-09-13 could not separate naturalness from comprehensibility. We keep them apart until each has its own operational rule.

candidates.mode: ordinal scale per note; not yet defined
candidates.applicability: Both languages, each with its own operationalisation: what reads as natural in Czech clinical writing is not a translation of the English rule. Requires human raters; no automatic proxy is proposed.

examples.positive: The note reads as a clinician wrote it, in the ordinary register of the language.
examples.negative: The note repeats one template phrase in every section and renders English idioms word for word in Czech.
examples.boundary: A note that is grammatical and comprehensible but stilted: comprehensibility (K13) passes and naturalness is the open question.

candidates.measurement: Not yet defined. A human rating scale written in both languages; perplexity or judge ratings are not evidence of naturalness until checked against human ratings.
candidates.error_consequence: Low for care; an unnatural note is still read. It marks the text as machine-written and can lower trust in the content.
candidates.validation: None on notes. Transfer evidence only: fluency is a separately annotated dimension in general summarisation evaluation (S8), and the PDSQI lineage folded it into comprehensibility (S2).
candidates.state_note: Returned by audit A07. A rating rule must be written in English and in Czech and assessed by humans before it can be measured.

candidates.label: Redundancy: the same fact more than once
candidates.definition: An essential information unit appears in the note more than once without new content. Not economy: a repeated sentence still carries content, so the share of content-bearing sentences (K11) does not see it. Not density: density also falls with padding that repeats nothing.
candidates.origin_note: The earlier criterion c15 named repetition explicitly. The review of 2026-09-13 merged it into K11, whose per-sentence definition cannot see a repeated relevant fact (audit A07). Restored on 2026-09-16 as its own candidate.

evidence.quote: A sentence is not concise if it does not cover any rubric items.
evidence.supports: Conciseness is defined per sentence by whether the sentence covers a rubric item; a second sentence covering the same item counts as concise.
evidence.our_adaptation: Repetition of a relevant fact is therefore invisible to K11 and needs its own construct.

evidence.quote: The summary is brief, to the point, and without redundancy
evidence.supports: Redundancy is part of the definition of the Succinct attribute.
evidence.our_adaptation: Rated there as one Likert item together with brevity; we keep repetition apart from economy.

evidence.quote: Tools for assessing note redundancy are required to complement use of the PDQI-9.
evidence.supports: The validation study measured redundancy with a separate automated score and named it a gap of the instrument.
evidence.our_adaptation: Their redundancy is copy-paste across notes of a record; ours is repetition within one note. The unit differs and the method does not transfer.

candidates.mode: count of repeated units per note, then a share; not yet defined
candidates.unit: information unit repeated within one note
candidates.applicability: Any note; needs the same unit bank as coverage. A restatement that adds a consequence, such as a next step, is not repetition.

examples.positive: Each essential unit appears once, in its section.
examples.negative: The client's panic attacks are described in Subjective, again in Assessment and again in Plan, with nothing new each time.
examples.boundary: A fact restated in Plan with a new next step attached is not repetition.

candidates.measurement: Not yet defined: the share of information units that appear more than once without added content. Unit boundaries and what counts as added content need rules and human checking.
candidates.error_consequence: Moderate: repetition lengthens the note, hides omissions behind volume and inflates any comparison that grows with length.
candidates.validation: None on generated notes. PDQI-9's validation measured copy-paste redundancy across notes with a separate score and named redundancy a gap of the instrument (S4).
candidates.state_note: Split from K11 by audit A07. The unit rules for repetition are not defined; measurable once the coverage bank of P01 exists.

candidates.label: Cultural competence evidenced in the note
candidates.definition: The note shows that the client's cultural, linguistic and social context was taken into account where it bore on the session: how the client's background is recorded, whether an adaptation or an interpreter is noted, and that no assumption about the client stands in for what was said. It is judged from the note alone, as what the note shows about the care.
candidates.origin_note: Found in TN-Eval's general items (Appendix A.5, 'Evidence of treatment being provided in a culturally competent manner'). The source-first extraction of 2026-09-20 left it open with a proposal not to adopt it, because it reads as a property of the care rather than of the note; the investigator decided on 2026-09-21 to adopt it.

evidence.quote: Evidence of treatment being provided in a culturally competent manner. Importance: Highly recommended
evidence.supports: Cultural competence is an item of the note rubric, graded highly recommended and applying across sections.
evidence.our_adaptation: TN-Eval treats it as something the note carries. Whether a note can show it without knowing the therapist's intent is the open operational question, and S1 reports no score for the item.

candidates.mode: human judgement; scale not yet defined
candidates.applicability: Where the session carries cultural, linguistic or social context that bore on the care. A session without such content makes the item not applicable, which is not a failure.

examples.positive: The note records that the client's religious framing of guilt was taken up in the intervention in the client's own terms.
examples.negative: The note explains the client's reluctance by a cultural stereotype the session does not contain.
examples.boundary: The transcript carries no cultural content; the note says nothing about it and the item is not applicable.

candidates.measurement: Not yet defined. Human rating only; needs a rule for when the item applies and for what counts as evidence, written in both languages.
candidates.error_consequence: A note that reads the client through a stereotype is read by the next clinician and by the client; the harm is to the relationship and to trust, and it is permanent.
candidates.validation: One rubric item in S1, never reported as a score there. No study found measures it in generated notes.
candidates.overlaps: K14 (stigmatising wording), K02 (originator of a statement), K27 (evenness across groups).
candidates.state_note: Adopted by the investigator on 2026-09-21 from an open source property. No rating rule exists in either language.

candidates.label: Internal consistency within one note
candidates.definition: No part of the note ignores or contradicts another part of the same note. Distinct from K26, which is consistency between notes of one case, and from K01: two statements can each have support in the source at different moments and still contradict each other when the note presents both as current.
candidates.origin_note: The PDQI-9 attribute 'Internally consistent' (S4, as reproduced in S6, Table 1). PDSQI-9 removed it as redundant (S2). The source-first extraction of 2026-09-20 found no candidate covering it; the investigator decided on 2026-09-21 to add it.

evidence.location: PDQI-9 form, item 9, as reproduced in S6 Table 1
evidence.quote: No part of the note ignores or contradicts any other part.
evidence.supports: Internal consistency is a rated attribute of the instrument family.
evidence.our_adaptation: Rated there as one Likert item over the whole note; we would locate each contradicting pair instead.

evidence.quote: Two PDQI-9 attributes, Up-to-Date and Consistent, were removed
evidence.supports: The successor instrument judged the attribute redundant.
evidence.our_adaptation: Recorded as an argument against, not as a reason to omit: the redundancy with accuracy holds only when every claim is checked against the source, which a reader of the note alone cannot do.

candidates.mode: categorical per pair of contradicting statements; not yet defined
candidates.unit: pair of statements within one note
candidates.applicability: Any note. A contradiction the client themselves voiced and the note reports as the client's is fidelity, not inconsistency.

examples.positive: The plan in the Plan section follows from the assessment above it.
examples.negative: The Subjective section says the client stopped drinking; the Plan section plans to reduce the drinking.
examples.boundary: The note reports that the client said two contradictory things in the session; that is faithful reporting, not an inconsistency of the note.

candidates.measurement: Not yet defined. Locate pairs of statements in the note that cannot both hold, count them per note, and have a person check each pair.
candidates.error_consequence: A reader who finds a contradiction cannot tell which part to trust and discounts the whole note.
candidates.validation: Rated in S4 and S6 as one Likert item of PDQI-9; dropped in S2. No study found measures it in generated notes.
candidates.state_note: Added by the investigator on 2026-09-21 from an open source property. The rule for what counts as a contradicting pair is not written.
candidates.decided_by_note: A pair of statements that cannot both hold as current is a contradiction whoever reads it; the transcript is not needed.

candidates.label: Correct and appropriate professional terminology
candidates.definition: The note names what happened in the words the profession uses, and uses them correctly: a term stands for what the term means, a lay paraphrase does not replace a term that carries clinical meaning, and no term is used that the session does not support. Distinct from K30, which is whether the text reads as a clinician of that language would write it: a fluent note can use the wrong term, and a correct term can sit in a stilted sentence. Distinct from K13, which is whether the intended reader understands it.
candidates.origin_note: Found on 2026-10-05 by the investigator, who objected that language naturalness is not the same thing as clinical language. The property was in the source-first table all along, inside a bundled property: S_abs_edit names terminology as one of three categories of what clinicians edit in AI-drafted documentation, and the property had been mapped to K22 as a typology of edits, which left terminology itself with no candidate.

evidence.quote: an inductive coding framework with 11 codes across 3 categories: clinical content, terminology, and language style
evidence.supports: Terminology is one of three categories of what clinicians change in an AI-drafted note, named apart from clinical content and from language style.
evidence.our_adaptation: The source counts edits in ambient documentation of general medicine; that terminology is a property a psychotherapy note can be rated on, and how, is our step.

evidence.quote: Clinicians added specialty-specific clinical details and terminology
evidence.supports: What the clinicians added was specialty-specific terminology, so the draft's terminology was not merely unnatural but absent or wrong for the setting.
evidence.our_adaptation: Read as evidence that terminology and genericness come apart: the same theme feeds K28. Which of the two a given edit repairs is not decided here.

candidates.mode: ordinal per note, or categorical per term; not yet defined
candidates.applicability: Both languages, each with its own rule: Czech clinical terminology is not a translation of the English list, and for the client purpose the requirement inverts, because a note a client reads should not lean on terms.

examples.positive: The note writes that the client reports early waking and loss of interest, and calls the latter anhedonia where the session's content supports it.
examples.negative: The note calls the client's described worry a panic attack, which the session does not describe.
examples.boundary: The note writes „the client was somehow out of it“: not a wrong term, a missing one, which is the same failure from the other side.

candidates.measurement: Not yet defined. A rating rule written in English and in Czech, applied by a clinician, distinguishing a wrong term, a missing term and an unsupported term. No automatic proxy is proposed: a term list would reward the word and not its use.
candidates.error_consequence: A wrong term is read by the next clinician as a finding, and a term the session does not support is a diagnosis nobody made. A missing term costs precision rather than safety.
candidates.validation: None on notes. The support is an edit-category analysis of general-medicine ambient documentation, read in full; no study rates terminology in psychotherapy notes.
candidates.overlaps: K30 (naturalness of the language), K13 (comprehensibility for the reader), K04 (certainty of a diagnostic statement), K01 (a term the source does not support).
candidates.state_note: Accepted by the investigator on 2026-10-05. No rating rule exists in either language, and a term list is explicitly not a substitute.

candidates.label: The interaction is described from both sides
candidates.definition: The note describes what the therapist did and how the client responded to it, not one without the other. The source's instrument orders this in four levels: the therapist's approach is missing or too thin to read; the approach is there but not the client's response; the approach is there and met practically, without reaching the client's experience or feelings; both the approach and the client's response are there. Distinct from K25, which asks whether a supervisor can tell what the therapist did and why: a note can answer that and still say nothing about what it did to the client. Distinct from K02, which is attribution, who said a thing: this is whether the exchange is there at all.
candidates.origin_note: Found on 2026-10-07 when SESPI was read in full. The property had been in the catalog since 2026-09-13 inside an abstract-only row, S_abs_sespi-a01, 'How staff-patient interactions are captured in progress notes', mapped to K25 and K02 as 'the interaction as content'. That mapping absorbed an instrument's central construct into two candidates that are not it. It is the second property found this way, after terminology inside S_abs_edit-p01, and both were found by reading a source rather than its abstract.

evidence.quote: In Step 3, the descriptions of staff-patient interactions are assessed by four alternatives: A. No or insufficient description of the staff's approach. B. The staff's approach is described, but the patient's response is not, or not sufficiently, described. C. The staff's approach is described, and the patient appears to experience it as fair enough. However, the approach is mostly oriented to practical solutions and fails to grasp the patient's experience or feelings. D. Both staff's approach and patient's response are described.
evidence.supports: A four-level ordinal rule over a mental health progress note, manualised, with the levels distinguished by which side of the interaction is present.
evidence.our_adaptation: The source scores excerpts of inpatient psychiatric notes written by nursing staff. That the same levels apply to a psychotherapy session note is shown by S21 and not by S20; that they apply to a model-written note is our step, and nothing in either source says a generated note fails these levels in the same way a hurried human note does.

evidence.location: Results, inter-rater and internal consistency for each step
evidence.quote: Cronbach's alpha for Step 3 was 0.970 and ICC was 0.968 (95% CI 0.929-0.991). The percentage agreement was high (84.1)
evidence.supports: Raters agree on the four levels: 84.1% absolute agreement across 22 raters, with an ICC above 0.9.
evidence.our_adaptation: The figure is for 22 raters scoring ten excerpts, which is a small number of observations for a reliability claim, and the source's own total ICC of 0.770 is far below its alpha of 0.977. We report the step figure with both cautions and do not carry it over to a judge model, which is not a human rater.

evidence.location: Results, Table 1, changes in described interaction
evidence.quote: Before the intervention, only 15% described an entire therapist-client interaction (T0), but this category increased to nearly 40% after the intervention (T1)
evidence.supports: In a psychotherapy service, most notes do not describe both sides: at T0, 49.3% of 193 notes were at level A and 15.1% at level D.
evidence.our_adaptation: A base rate, which is why the property can separate notes rather than being passed by everything. It is a base rate for human therapists in one Norwegian municipal service, and what models do is the thing to be measured.

candidates.mode: ordinal, four levels, from the source's manual
candidates.unit: the note, or an excerpt of it; the instrument was tested on excerpts and the 2025 application scored whole journal notes, so which unit a level belongs to is not settled by the source and has to be declared
candidates.applicability: Both languages. The rule reads the note alone, so it needs no transcript, which also means it cannot tell a described interaction from an invented one: a model that writes a plausible exchange that did not happen scores D here and fails K01.

examples.positive: The note records that the therapist named the client's silence and asked what it was protecting, and that the client said it felt safer not to answer yet.
examples.negative: The note records that the therapist worked on the client's avoidance, and says nothing about how the client took it.
examples.boundary: The note records that the client asked for a letter for their employer and that the therapist agreed to write one. The approach is practical and the client accepted it, and the client's experience of the session is absent: the source's level C rather than D.

candidates.measurement: Not measured in this round. The rule exists and is manualised, so what is missing is a decision to measure it, not a definition.
candidates.error_consequence: Scored from the note alone, a confident invention of an exchange is indistinguishable from an accurate record of one. The level must never be read as evidence that the interaction happened, and must be reported beside K01.
candidates.validation: SESPI Step 3: Cronbach's alpha 0.970, ICC 0.968 (95% CI 0.929-0.991), 84.1% absolute agreement, 22 raters, 10 excerpts (S20). No human anchor of our own, and no figure for a judge model.
candidates.overlaps: K25 (what a supervisor can tell the therapist did and why), K02 (attribution of who said what), K36 (whether the client's experience is described at all, which is the gate this rule sits behind in the source), K01 (whether the described exchange is supported by the session).
candidates.state_note: Arrived on 2026-10-07, after protocol 2.7.0 froze the round's measured set at 16 and after the pilot's jobs were planned. It is in the pool the panel rates under D13; whether it is measured follows from the panel's rating and a later protocol amendment, not from this entry.

candidates.label: The client's experience is in the note, not only their behaviour
candidates.definition: The note carries some description of how the client experienced something, and not only what the client was observed to do. The source's instrument asks this as a yes-or-no gate before anything else is scored, and its own example of a no is a note that reports only conduct. Distinct from K05, which asks whether the substantive content of the session is there: a note can cover the session's topics completely and report none of the client's experience of them. Distinct from K28, which asks whether what is there is specific to this client rather than generic.
candidates.origin_note: Found on 2026-10-07 with K35, in the same abstract-only row that had absorbed the whole of SESPI into K25 and K02.

evidence.quote: In Step 1, all excerpts are scored dichotomously: “Does the excerpt contain some kind of description of patient's experience?” A yes means proceed to Step 2; a no signifies no further assessment of that excerpt. A typical example that would be scored “no” is “Mostly stayed in his room. He answers briefly when the staff poses specific questions.”
evidence.supports: The presence of the client's experience is a property an instrument scores on its own, dichotomously, and its absence is a recognisable kind of note rather than an oversight.
evidence.our_adaptation: The source uses it as a gate: an excerpt scored no is excluded from the rest of the instrument. We would report it as a property in its own right and must not use it as a gate, because excluding the notes that fail it is how a corpus mean comes to describe only the notes that passed.

evidence.location: Results, inter-rater and internal consistency for each step
evidence.quote: The internal consistency reliability was very high (Kuder-Richardson 20 for Step 1 = 0.984). The absolute inter-rater agreement for all scores ( N = 10 scores per rater) was very high (95.9%
evidence.supports: Raters agree almost completely on whether a note describes the client's experience.
evidence.our_adaptation: The source itself cautions that the figure must be read with care because the scale is dichotomous, and the observations are ten. We keep the caution with the figure.

candidates.mode: dichotomous in the source; an ordinal form is possible and is not the source's
candidates.unit: the note, or an excerpt of it; the same unresolved unit as K35
candidates.applicability: Both languages. Read from the note alone, so as with K35 it cannot distinguish a described experience from an invented one.

examples.positive: The note records that the client said the week felt like wading, and that getting up was the hardest part of the day.
examples.negative: The note records that the client attended, spoke little and left on time.
examples.boundary: The note records a diagnosis-shaped summary, that the client presented with low mood and reduced motivation, and nothing of how the client described it. Whether clinical wording of a state counts as the client's experience is the judgement the rule has to settle, and the source settles it by asking for the client's own experience.

candidates.measurement: Not measured in this round, for the same reason as K35.
candidates.error_consequence: Used as a gate, as the source uses it, it removes the worst notes from every other measure. Reported as a property, its cost is only that a note of pure conduct is marked as such.
candidates.validation: SESPI Step 1: Kuder-Richardson 20 = 0.984, ICC 0.982 (95% CI 0.959-0.995), 95.9% absolute agreement, 22 raters, 10 excerpts, with the source's own caution about a dichotomous scale (S20).
candidates.overlaps: K05 (coverage of the session's substantive content), K28 (personalisation), K35 (the two-sided description of the interaction, which the source gates behind this), K04 (the certainty status of a statement about the client's state).
candidates.state_note: Arrived on 2026-10-07 with K35 and is in the pool the panel rates under D13. The source's gate design is the reason it is written as a property here and not as a filter.

methods.label: QA against a bank built from the source
methods.what: Before the note is seen, questions on the essential information are created from the source. The answerer receives only the note. The answers are compared with the answers from the source.
methods.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal, recorded before this review. Finding QuestEval and QAFactEval does not retroactively change its origin; it only gives it later methodological support.
methods.limits: Measures only what the bank asks. An unanswered question can mean an omission, an ambiguity or a failure of the answerer; those are three different outcomes. QuestEval and QAFactEval are validated on English news text, not on clinical text and not in Czech.

methods.label: Verification of atomic claims against the source
methods.what: The note is decomposed into atomic claims and each is verified against the source.
methods.origin_note: Existed in the project as reverse-claims. FActScore is a later methodological support.
methods.limits: Measures precision, not omission; on its own it cannot replace ME01. The atomicity of the decomposition is itself an unverified step: full character coverage does not prove that the claims are actually atomic.

methods.label: Rubric item coverage with graded importance
methods.what: For every rubric item it is determined whether it is in the corresponding section of the note, and the score is reported separately by importance level.
methods.origin_note: From TN-Eval. Our current implementation ignores the importance levels.
methods.limits: TN-Eval itself shows that an LLM judge is usable for coverage; the same does not hold for the other dimensions. Requires a rubric with assigned importance, which we do not have for Czech.

methods.label: Mapping sentences to content units
methods.what: Every sentence of the note is labelled with the content units it carries; a sentence without a unit is superfluous.
methods.limits: In TN-Eval this is the dimension where the automatic judge correlates worst with humans. Reporting it alone means rewarding an empty note.

methods.label: Typology of fidelity errors
methods.what: A finding is not classified merely as an error but by kind: invented, distorted, no error.
methods.limits: The typology has three levels and is probably insufficient for our purposes: it does not distinguish errors in actor, time and modality, which matter for a psychotherapy note.

methods.label: Alignment score without a judge
methods.what: Fidelity is computed by an alignment model, not by a language-model judge.
methods.origin_note: TN-Eval uses AlignScore precisely because the judge fails on fidelity.
methods.limits: An English model. For Czech a replacement would have to be found and verified; that is separate work, not a parameter.

methods.label: Contradiction detection with inference models
methods.what: Inconsistency is sought by classifying the relation between source and claim.
methods.origin_note: Found only in the audit of the below-threshold stratum, i.e. outside the priority screen.
methods.limits: VERIFIED FROM THE TITLE AND ABSTRACT ONLY. English benchmarks.

methods.label: Checking authored citations
methods.what: For citations written in the note, the validity of the target, the actual support of the claim and the share of claims that carry a citation are checked separately.
methods.origin_note: Historically a colleague's proposal to link claims to the source.
methods.limits: The three numbers must not be merged. An incomplete citation check must not report 100%.

methods.label: Likert rating of attributes
methods.what: A professional rates the note on five-point scales by attribute.
methods.limits: Without rater training there is a risk of failure: r = 0.07 in Walker (untrained) against ICC 0.867 in PDSQI-9 (trained) are, however, different instruments, samples and statistics, so the comparison does not establish the effect of training. A high Cronbach's alpha (0.93) says nothing about agreement.

methods.label: Reference overlap with a human note
methods.what: ROUGE, BERTScore and similar metrics against a reference note.
methods.origin_note: Already running in the project on the iCARE track.
methods.limits: Measures none of the constructs of this registry. PDSQI-9 says so explicitly and MentalCLOUDS shows the divergence between these metrics and expert judgement on the same data. Keep as a descriptive figure, not as a measure of quality.

methods.label: Task-based human evaluation
methods.what: A person receives the note and has to do with it what the note is for.
methods.origin_note: Walker et al. asked a task question beside the scales; TN-Eval has an acceptance item.
methods.limits: Cannot be replaced by a judge. It is the only method that measures the purpose directly, and at the same time the most expensive. TN-Eval reports USD 190 for its whole human evaluation of notes, not for one task.

methods.label: Acceptability framework
methods.what: A professional rates the note on acceptability parameters that are not properties of the text.
methods.limits: Five of the six parameters cannot be derived from the text. Mixing them with textual scales would produce a meaningless score.

methods.label: Analysis of actual edits
methods.what: The model's draft is compared with what the professional finally saved, and the edits are sorted by kind.
methods.origin_note: A new finding of this round, read in full on 2026-09-20.
methods.limits: Read in full on 2026-09-20: eleven codes in three categories with interrater reliability, synthesised into five themes. Requires real operation, which we do not have. Zero edits do not mean quality; they can mean no time to check.

methods.label: Classification of error severity
methods.what: Every finding receives a severity grade according to the possible clinical consequence, not according to how many characters are wrong.
methods.origin_note: Walker et al. asked about major or minor errors; studies on AI scribes report error severity separately.
methods.limits: Requires clinical judgement of the consequence, which cannot be derived from the text. Without it a rare severe error drowns among ordinary ones.

methods.label: Consensus construction of criteria
methods.what: Criteria and their importance are set by structured expert consensus.
methods.origin_note: PDSQI-9 used a semi-Delphi; TN-Eval a two-step co-design with five therapists and verification with seventeen more.
methods.limits: This is the step that is entirely missing for Czech. One investigator with AI assistance does not replace it.

methods.label: Breakdown of results by subgroup
methods.what: Existing scores are broken down by client group, language variety or topic.
methods.origin_note: A new finding of this round.
methods.limits: Not a new measure, a different view of existing ones. Requires enough cases per subgroup; infeasible with one Czech client cluster.

methods.label: Linguistic diversity as an indicator of personalisation
methods.what: It is computed how much the notes of one system resemble each other: semantically by the mean cosine similarity of sentences to the centroid, superficially by mean pairwise self-ROUGE. Lower similarity means higher diversity.
methods.origin_note: Found only while tracing the full text of S19, in its open-access companion work.
methods.limits: A proxy, not a measurement of personalisation. The authors themselves report that the semantic variant depends on the embedding model chosen and gave an inconsistent picture. High diversity can also mean hallucination or incoherent text, so it may be read only for notes that have already passed the fidelity check. Not verified for Czech.

levels.label: Text span / character range
levels.gap: Outside citations we cannot say which words of the source support a claim. For human checking that is exactly the most useful unit.

levels.label: Session segment (e.g. a five-minute segment)
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. The most directly relevant work found (S19) evaluates exactly at this unit: 108 five-minute segments from 36 sessions. It yields far more observations from the same material than whole-note evaluation, and we do not use it at all.

levels.label: Sentence of the note
levels.gap: Covered, but only for economy. The sentence as a unit of error is not used.

levels.label: Atomic claim
levels.gap: Covered. The atomicity of the decomposition is itself unverified.

levels.label: Information unit from the source
levels.gap: Covered, but without graded importance and without any check of what the bank did not ask.

levels.label: Section of the note
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. In TN-Eval the experts agreed perfectly on which section a rubric item belongs to (during rubric design, not while rating notes); placement is therefore well defined, and we do not measure it.

levels.label: Series of notes of one case
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. Continuity of care is a declared purpose, and nothing measures the relation between a note and the previous one. This is the largest structural gap.

levels.label: The case as a whole
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. We cannot say whether the documentation of a case makes sense as a whole.

levels.label: Generator across cases
levels.by: aggregation in the leaderboard; newly ME17
levels.gap: We aggregate scores but do not measure systematic tendency: what a given model always leaves out. ME17 offers a method for one such property (genericness); the rest remains uncovered.

levels.label: Client subgroup or language variety
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. Inequality of quality across groups is invisible at the level of one note.

levels.label: Rater and rating conditions
levels.gap: We track the judge's identity and settings, but not the training of human raters, which according to Walker decides whether the instrument works at all.

levels.label: The decision that rests on the note
levels.gap: NOT COVERED. We do not ask whether the note supports a concrete decision, only whether it contains content.

blind_spots.label: Contradiction between sessions
blind_spots.example: The note of session 5 says the client mentioned panic attacks for the first time. The note of session 3 already describes them. Both notes are fully faithful to their own transcripts.
blind_spots.why_invisible: Every candidate of the previous map asks about one note against one source. The contradiction lies between two notes, where no item reaches.

blind_spots.label: Correct content in the wrong section
blind_spots.example: The therapist's interpretation is written in the Subjective section as if it were the client's statement. The information is in the note, so coverage is full and so is fidelity.
blind_spots.why_invisible: Coverage asks whether the information is there. It does not ask where. And it was exactly the placement of items into sections that the TN-Eval experts agreed on during rubric design.

blind_spots.label: Missing what the bank never asked
blind_spots.example: In the session the client mentions stopping their medication. The question bank does not ask about medication because nobody marked it as essential. Coverage comes out at 100%.
blind_spots.why_invisible: QA measures only what it asks. The map has no item for checking the completeness of the bank itself.
blind_spots.needs: human check of the information bank; ME15

blind_spots.label: A faithful and yet harmful note
blind_spots.example: The note quotes verbatim what the client said about their daughter's sexual orientation. The quotation is accurate, supported, correctly attributed and unnecessary for the purpose of the note.
blind_spots.why_invisible: The fidelity family gives such a note full marks. The harm arises precisely through the accuracy.

blind_spots.label: A manufactured negative finding
blind_spots.example: The note says Suicidal ideation: denied. Nobody asked about it in the session.
blind_spots.why_invisible: A presence check sees a filled field. A fidelity check has nothing to compare, because the source contains neither the statement nor its denial.

blind_spots.label: Systematic inequality across clients
blind_spots.example: For clients speaking non-standard Czech the model reliably omits the content of the Assessment section. Every single note looks average.
blind_spots.why_invisible: The map has no level above one note. The inequality is visible only in a breakdown across dozens of cases.

blind_spots.label: The missing note
blind_spots.example: The model does not answer for a given session, or refuses. The note does not exist.
blind_spots.why_invisible: Every item of the map rates text. Non-existent text has no score, and if it is dropped from the denominator it raises the average of the model that failed.
blind_spots.needs: Reporting planned, usable and assessed units separately.

blind_spots.label: A citation that points correctly and does not support
blind_spots.example: A claim cites an existing turn in the transcript. The turn is about a different topic.
blind_spots.why_invisible: The validity check of the target passes. Without a separate check of semantic support this becomes a supported claim.

blind_spots.label: A note good for one purpose and unusable for another
blind_spots.example: The note is excellent for continuity: dense, professional, full of abbreviations. As a client summary it is unreadable.
blind_spots.why_invisible: A single overall quality score averages this contradiction away and hides it. That is exactly why no overall score is computed.

blind_spots.label: A note that would fit anyone
blind_spots.example: The note says the client showed anxiety, reflected on their situation and was motivated to change. Every statement is supported, nothing essential is missing, the sections fit. The same text would pass unchanged for half of the other sessions.
blind_spots.why_invisible: Fidelity, coverage, organisation and economy all give full marks. Genericness can be recognised only by comparison with the other notes of the same system, a level the map did not have.

blind_spots.label: Silent editing instead of rejection
blind_spots.example: The therapist accepts the note, but first rewrites three of its four sections. The resulting documentation is fine.
blind_spots.why_invisible: What gets rated is the final text or the acceptance. The amount of work the acceptance cost appears nowhere.

pilot_proposal.status: AI proposal; no human selection decision has been made

entries.label: Coverage of essential content, separately by importance level
entries.why: The strongest documented change against the current state and at the same time the core of the continuity purpose. It carries K07 as a reporting rule (coverage per purpose, never summed) and K10 as the plan importance level.
entries.human_input: A therapist must approve the information bank and assign the importance levels.
entries.risk: Without a Czech rubric with importance this is so far only a transfer of the English one. Always reported together with P14; coverage alone rewards longer text.
entries.saturation_detail: TN-Eval completeness: humans 29.5% (SD 12.4), Llama 39.7 (7.9), Mistral 38.1 (7.5). At a fifth to two fifths of the ceiling. Of all measured quantities it has the most room and nobody has hit the ceiling anywhere yet.

entries.label: Distinguishing missing information, explicit negation and not asked
entries.why: A repeatedly found weakness of our own project; without it false negative findings are manufactured.
entries.human_input: A therapist judges the disputed cases.
entries.risk: The boundary between not asked and implicit negation is unclear and will be disputed.
entries.saturation_detail: Nobody has ever measured this triad separately. There is not a single number. Our own reviews, however, repeatedly found models manufacturing the gap as a negative finding, so the phenomenon exists.

entries.label: Coverage of risk content as an undilutable layer
entries.why: The highest error consequence. Rarity is not a reason to drop it.
entries.human_input: A therapist marks the risk-related units and judges severity.
entries.risk: A rare phenomenon; in a small pilot it will have a wide interval and that must be reported.
entries.saturation_detail: Safety is the only mandatory general item in TN-Eval, but nobody reported its coverage separately. Rarity means a wide interval in a small pilot; under the protocol it is not a reason for exclusion.

entries.label: Support of claims with four outcomes and an error type
entries.why: The core of a note's credibility; the method is implemented in the project.
entries.human_input: A therapist verifies a sample of the verdicts.
entries.risk: The decomposition into claims is itself an unverified step.
entries.saturation: ceiling in sight, yet it still discriminates
entries.saturation_detail: Keren: clinicians 4.80 of 5 (SD 0.25), model 4.20 (0.49). High near the ceiling, and yet the largest effect of all three dimensions, d = 1.54. TN-Eval on a different unit: 87.0 vs 68.5 and 71.8, far from the ceiling. Saturation therefore depends on the unit, not on the construct.

entries.label: Errors in actor, time and modality as separate types
entries.why: The three-way TN-Eval typology does not distinguish these, and for psychotherapy they matter more than for general text.
entries.human_input: A therapist judges whether the distinction is meaningful in practice.
entries.risk: It may turn out that the types do not occur separately in real data.
entries.saturation_detail: Keren describe that the error type differs by component and that the model attributed interventions to the therapist that were not performed, but nobody reported these types as separate numbers.

entries.label: Placement of content in the expected section
entries.why: In TN-Eval five experts agreed perfectly on which section a rubric item belongs to (agreement during rubric design, not validation of P06 on actual notes). Placement is therefore well defined and today we do not measure it at all.
entries.human_input: A therapist confirms the section mapping for the Czech tasks.
entries.risk: Applies only to tasks with a prescribed structure.
entries.saturation_detail: The experts had PERFECT agreement on where content belongs. How often the models confuse it, however, nobody has measured. The highest ratio of measurement reliability to cost.

entries.label: Share of content-bearing sentences, always reported beside coverage
entries.why: Implemented; the main change is the ban on reporting it alone.
entries.risk: According to TN-Eval this is the dimension where automation agrees worst with humans.
entries.saturation: ceiling in sight for good models
entries.saturation_detail: TN-Eval conciseness: humans 75.6 (14.9), Llama 84.0 (12.1), Mistral 91.5 (SD 7.1). Mistral is at the ceiling and the spread narrows. Among strong models it will soon stop discriminating.

entries.label: Stigmatising wording, distinguishing quotation from the author's text
entries.why: The only attribute PDSQI introduced explicitly because of model behaviour.
entries.human_input: A therapist must approve the Czech formulations; a dictionary filter is inadmissible.
entries.risk: No support exists for Czech. The highest risk of a wrong transfer.
entries.saturation_detail: PDSQI introduced the attribute because of model behaviour but did not report the score distribution. Zero data for Czech.

entries.label: Taking over care: would the note carry continuation without the transcript
entries.format: yes / no / cannot decide plus justification
entries.why: The only measurement that asks directly about the purpose. Without it the whole benchmark is a proxy.
entries.human_input: Therapists as raters, trained on the instrument.
entries.risk: The most expensive pilot item. TN-Eval reports USD 190 for its whole human evaluation of notes, not for one task; P10 must be budgeted from its own procedure (measured time per note).
entries.saturation_detail: Walker asked this question but did not report its distribution. The related TN-Eval acceptance item: human notes 2.34 of 5, Llama 3.34, Mistral 3.73. Far from the ceiling and discriminates strongly.

entries.label: Acceptability of the note for practice on six parameters
entries.why: MentalCLOUDS showed that expert judgement diverges from automatic metrics; without this measurement we will not see that divergence.
entries.human_input: Therapists; the parameters must be translated and verified.
entries.risk: Five of the six parameters are not properties of the text; they must not be mixed with textual scales.
entries.saturation_detail: MentalCLOUDS used the six parameters but did not report numbers per parameter; it states only that Mistral outperformed the others and that room for improvement remains on opportunity costs and perceived effectiveness.

entries.label: Control measurement of agreement between trained and untrained raters
entries.why: Walker versus PDSQI suggests that whether the instrument works at all rests on this difference. Measuring it here is cheap and it decides the validity of everything else.
entries.risk: Requires more raters than the pilot counted on. Can be limited to a subsample.
entries.saturation_detail: Untrained raters: r = 0.07 (p = 0.270) and an inability to tell a good note from a poor one, F(3,34) = 1.15, p = 0.342. Trained: ICC 0.867 in PDSQI and ICC 0.81 / 0.71 / 0.65 in Keren. These are, however, different instruments, samples, raters and statistics: the comparison recommends training; it establishes neither its causal effect nor its size (audit A06). The size of the difference in the pilot is measured, not assumed.

entries.label: Diversity of one system's notes as an indicator of genericness
entries.unit: the set of notes of one generator
entries.why: Catches a type of failure no other proposed measurement sees: a note that is faithful, complete and well organised, and would nevertheless fit anyone.
entries.human_input: A therapist judges whether systems with low diversity really read as generic.
entries.risk: An exploratory diagnostic, not established personalisation: high diversity can reflect errors and low diversity genuinely similar sessions. It depends on the embedding model, requires the same cases and model version across systems, human checks of source-specific detail, and disclosure of any faithfulness-based selection of notes. Genericness can also be examined within one note against its source (audit A08).
entries.saturation: unknown, and the measure itself is fragile
entries.saturation_detail: Klein: humans had higher linguistic diversity, but the authors admit that the semantic variant changed with the embedding model chosen and gave an inconsistent picture.

entries.label: Information density and comparison at aligned length
entries.format: continuous ratio: distinct essential information units per language-specific length unit
entries.why: A construct in its own right, not an addendum to coverage. Without it the benchmark systematically rewards length, which is exactly the tendency models have, so the error always points one way.
